Murphey begins his Boxing Day diatribe with the following statement:

The Liberal government does not have the right to change Canada’s voting system without first holding a referendum. The notion that we can fundamentally alter our democracy without subjecting the change to a full public consultation is simply wrong, as voting is not a privilege granted by a political party to the people — it is the people who vest power, for a limited time, in a political party. It is up to the voters to decide how they shall choose which party to give that power to.

He is wrong. There may be those who believe that he is right, but they are also wrong.

The Constitution says that we have the right to vote for members of the House of Commons at least once every five years (unless it is "in time of real or apprehended war, invasion or insurrection" in which case that period can be extended), and as far as voting rights go that's pretty well it. It would be nice if the either the constitution or federal law addressed the issue of national referendums on significant government decisions - but it doesn't, and since no government to date has had the fortitude to introduce such legislation here we are.

(Little known fact: It wasn't until the 3rd General Election in 1874 that Canadians were granted the privilege of a secret ballot - and that's not constitutional law, it was a federal statute which, being what it is, could theoretically be repealed.)

Democracy, as defined by Oxford is

A system of government by the whole population or all the eligible members of a state, typically through elected representatives

That is not going to change under some form of proportional representation. In fact with proportional representation we will have parliaments that are actually reflective of how the population voted in any given election - we do not have that now.

No, as much as Rex Murphey and others may want to believe that the federal government does not have the right to modify the electoral system it would seem that it does in fact have that power; and quite frankly I am hoping that they exercise it and that our most recent election is in fact the last election conducted under an antiquated electoral system where fuzzy electoral math magically morphs the greatest minority into a majority.

In closing let me offer Mr. Murphey something that is a fact. Regardless of what FPTP electoral math may want us to believe 39.5 does not equal 54.

I believe that most reasonable Canadians know that, and further believe (unless they have supped too deeply of the kool-aid of conspiracy theorists who believe that this change is a coup designed to keep the Liberals in power forever) those same Canadians would agree that any electoral math that changes that is a welcome change.
Dear Rex Murphey, an opinion formed as a statement does not make a fact
